transcript:
Meeting header: 2028-06-21 15:30 UTC — Duration 72m. Attendees: Chris Mason (Redwood AE), Priya Kapoor (Redwood SE), Maya Chen (Cobalt ML Infra lead), Omar Reyes (CTO), Lena Park (SRE).

Summary (auto): Deep technical profiling session focusing on interleaved kernel execution behavior when using CUDA Graph capture vs dynamic launch. Discussed kv cache interactions, batching strategies, quantization impacts on kernel fusion, and on-prem / VPC profiling constraints.

00:00:12 Chris: hey everyone thanks for joining, um let's do quick intros. i'm chris mason, i'm the AE on this deal. priya's gonna run the deep profiling bits.
00:00:22 Priya: hi all, priya kapoor, inference systems se. we'll jump into traces and then sketch an experiment plan.
00:00:30 Maya: maya here, i own infra for models at cobalt. quick note: we run a mix of prod hosted and a private cluster behind our vpc, two rtx-a100 nodes in the on-prem rack.
00:00:42 Omar: and i'm omar cto, mainly here for architecture constraints and SLA talk.
00:00:46 Lena: lena, sre. i'll coordinate access and timing for profiling.

00:01:12 Chris: cool. high level objective — customer sees intermittent tail-latency spikes on our hosted inference, and in private runs we saw kernel path divergence when using cudagraph capture. priya, you saw the traces we uploaded?
00:01:27 Priya: yeah, i pulled the nvtx stacks, and a quick caveat — some of the names in the capture got mangled by the agent so you'll see weird labels, i think cup ti sampling mixed with nvprof, which makes the capture noisy. first observation: when using CUDA Graph capture on the seq-512 workload we have long contiguous kernels that look fused, but on longer sequences or when kv cache miss churn happens, the runtime falls back to dynamic launches mid-capture which causes a lot of stream serialization.
00:02:06 Maya: that's our symptom – throughput is fine, but 95/99 latency jumps during regen flows. we suspected kv cache eviction.
00:02:14 Priya: eviction is likely – i see small bursts where kv cache gets cold and we get extra memcpy + kernel prep which cudagraph capture didn't anticipate. cudagraphs shine when execution pattern is stable, but with interleaved kv op patterns capture can lead to graph replay that serializes.
00:02:35 Omar: can you define "serializes"? like it blocks the whole lane?
00:02:39 Priya: right, so when the capture replays a graph it schedules a set of kernels onto a stream as a single node; if a dynamic event happens — e.g., a new kv miss forces an additional kernel on a different stream — the driver enforces ordering which can stall other lanes, causing head-of-line latency. it's not always a full block but enough to bounce 99th.
00:03:05 Lena: interesting, we saw something similar in our early tests but attributed it to numa/pcie contention. is that different?
00:03:11 Priya: NUMA and PCIe contention are additive. when cudagraph capture reduces CPU overhead it can expose NVLink/PCIe hot spots, especially during memcpy-heavy kv swap. in your rack with two A100s, if the KV prefetch crosses NVLink hops unpredictably, you get extra memory staging, which combined with capture replay ordering amplifies the spike.
00:03:38 Chris: ok let's dig into the traces. priya you pulled the nvtx timeline — any obvious kernel candidates?
00:03:44 Priya: there are three hot kernels: 1) forward attention (fused matmul + softmax), 2) kv encode/pack, and 3) kv scatter/gather memcpy kernels. In the cudagraph captures the forward attention looks fused and occupies long contiguous time, but around the 0.62s mark we see a tiny memcpy kick off on stream 2 and then a new small kernel on stream 3 which causes cudaGraphReplay to enqueue a barrier. After that we see a 40–120ms tail blip.
00:04:18 Maya: that matches our telemetry windows, about 80–120ms spikes.
00:04:22 Omar: how is this different in vllm-based dynamic execution?
00:04:26 Priya: vLLM-style runtime tends to prefer many small dynamic launches and careful use of worker threads to hide memcpys; it doesn't rely on long monolithic graphs. That gives more flexibility for kv prefetch because you can interleave memcpy on separate streams and use fine-grained kernel ordering, but it costs more CPU overhead per token and can reduce aggregate throughput. So tradeoff: cudagraph gives throughput + lower CPU, but brittle to dynamic kv churn; dynamic exec gives stable tail but higher cost.
00:05:02 Chris: we should also call out quantization. did the int8 path change behavior?
00:05:08 Priya: yeah int8 kernels here are slightly different — TensorRT-LLM (tensorrtllm) generates specialized fused kernels that compress matmul+gelu into one operator; that's great for throughput, but those fused kernels have different memory access patterns and sometimes require extra workspace staging. On int8 traces the mem stage moved earlier and increased sensitivity to KV prefetch timing; in other words, fusion changed where the bottleneck sits.
00:05:40 Lena: so switching to int8 could make us more brittle?
00:05:44 Priya: possible. It can reduce token cost dramatically but may increase tail sensitivity to memory jitter. We saw a case where int8 fused kernel was 30% faster median but 2x worse 99th under high kv churn.
00:06:00 Maya: polarization — for production we want predictable 99th < 300ms. Our median is fine. Any mitigation patterns?
00:06:07 Priya: yes, a few options: 1) hybrid execution: capture stable prefix with cudagraph but fall back to dynamic launches for unlocked/variable suffixes; 2) pre-warm KV cache for heavy prompts; 3) adjust cudagraph capture boundaries—capture per-token micro-graphs instead of full sequence; 4) stager threads that pre-serialize memcpy onto dedicated streams before graph replay.
00:06:39 Omar: what's the cost of hybrid execution complexity-wise?
00:06:43 Priya: it's moderate. You need a routing policy in the runtime: if request looks like regen or has token variability > threshold, route to a dynamic path. Otherwise route to a captured-graph path. We have implemented heuristics in Redwood's runtime to do exactly that — these heuristics require a small amount of warmup metrics but are effective. There is engineering cost but low operational cost once in place.
00:07:05 Chris: does Redwood's private package support toggling this via config?
00:07:09 Priya: yes — in Dedicated/Private you can set capture_mode: hybrid|full|off and have fallbacks. We'll share the config docs.
00:07:17 Maya: let's talk about measurement — you're recommending NVTX + CUPTI traces. how intrusive are those?
00:07:23 Priya: nvtx is non-intrusive and cheap; cup ti sampling is more expensive and can perturb timing if sampling at high frequency. Capture best practice: 1) record NVTX and lightweight CUPTI traces at low sampling rate, 2) run deterministic replay when possible, 3) for binary-level behavior use nsight systems on one node for a few minutes, not continuous. Also collect per-token timestamps from the runtime to correlate.
00:07:51 Lena: we have strict maintenance windows. how long do you need for the on-prem run?
00:07:55 Priya: 2 hours should be enough — one short warmup + two profile runs (cudagraph vs dynamic) across your seq distribution. We'll need ephemeral access to one GPU host and the model artifact.
00:08:07 Chris: mentioned earlier we saw stream serialization. is there any kernel-level change we can apply, like reordering memcpy to a different stream or using cudaMemcpyAsync with pinning?
00:08:16 Priya: yes, pinning host buffers and using dedicated DMA streams for kv I/O helps. Also, isolating large memcpy off primary compute stream reduces interference. For cudagraphs specifically, ensure the capture includes the memcpy step or explicitly mark the memcpy as external and queue it before replay. That prevents unexpected dynamic memcpys during replay.
00:08:39 Omar: what about prefetch strategies in the runtime? we do some naive lookahead. is more aggressive prefetch always better?
00:08:45 Priya: not always — overly aggressive prefetch increases memory pressure and can cause eviction leading to the exact problem. The right approach is workload-aware prefetch: use request histograms to decide lookahead depth. For sparse regeneration flows, prefetch only the next N tokens where N is tuned per model and instance memory capacity. We'll help with tuning.
00:09:07 Maya: can the runtime predict regen vs forward-only? our prompts are conversational and sometimes regen is frequent.
00:09:13 Priya: we have lightweight heuristics: if request has stop tokens or callback patterns we flag as regen; also sequence length and user-mode (chat vs streaming) can be signals. Not perfect but reduces misroutes.
00:09:27 Chris: switching gears — you mentioned NUMA and PCIe earlier. how to detect if those are adding jitter?
00:09:33 Priya: check per-GPU memcpy times and compare local vs peer-to-peer times. If peer-to-peer over NVLink is being used, you should see lower latencies than going through host PCIe; if not, you may have topology misconfig or driver config forcing pageable transfers. Nsight systems can show link utilization. Also kernel scheduling stalls aligned with PCIe spikes indicate DMA contention.
00:09:58 Lena: we can run a quick script to dump p2p topology and run a memcpy microbench while collecting iostat and nvlink counters.
00:10:05 Priya: perfect. we'll share the microbench script.
00:10:10 Maya: any quick wins to lower 99th until we profile?
00:10:13 Priya: immediate mitigations: 1) temporarily disable cudagraphs for models with high kv churn (config capture_mode: off), 2) increase kv cache size if memory permits, 3) enable pinned memory for host->device transfers, 4) limit batch coalescing for regen flows so they don't trigger large combined memcpys.
00:10:32 Omar: do any of these require redeploy?
00:10:35 Priya: 1 and 4 are runtime config toggles — no image change. 2 requires instance memory increase. 3 is a runtime switch but may need restart to allocate pinned pools. We'll detail steps.
00:10:47 Chris: let's capture the experiment plan now.
00:10:50 Priya: plan: step A — baseline collection: one-hour telemetry from prod-like traffic; Maya will provide 48-hour trace but we want a targeted one-hour window to reproduce. Step B — small on-prem profiling window (2 hours) with nvtx + nsight on one host: run three modes: cudagraph full, cudagraph hybrid, dynamic. Step C — int8 vs fp16 runs to measure fusion impact. Step D — tweak prefetch policy and rerun to observe 99th delta. We'll produce a short report with flame timelines and per-kernel histograms.
00:11:24 Maya: agreed. we'll aim to provide traces by friday.
00:11:28 Lena: i'll set up ephemeral access and sync with chris.

00:11:40 [slight crosstalk]

00:12:02 Priya: a few more nitty-gritty things — when you capture, set environment to disable MPS for the profiling runs; MPS can reorder streams in a way that hides serialization in dev but not in prod, and vice versa. Also check driver ver — we saw differences across 525 vs 535 branches where cudagraph semantics changed subtly.
00:12:26 Omar: we run 535.12 currently. is that okay?
00:12:29 Priya: 535 is fine but we'll annotate known driver-specific caveats in the doc. Another footnote: TensorRT-LLM's optimizer sometimes fuses patterns differently across versions — include engine version in the trace metadata.
00:12:44 Chris: any security or compliance blockers for Redwood profiling inside their VPC?
00:12:49 Lena: we'll create ephemeral management bastion and restrict to internal IPs; data never leaves network. we require an NDA addendum?
00:12:57 Chris: we can sign the addendum. data handling notes: Redwood will not persist model artifacts beyond profiling window and will delete traces within 7 days. we'll put that in email.

00:13:12 Priya: last technical tidbit — consider micro-graphing: instead of capturing a whole token step, capture micro-graphs per attention block; this trades some overhead but gives you combinatorial flexibility to reorder without global barriers. It's a middle ground between full cudagraph and fully dynamic.
00:13:34 Maya: micro-graphing sounds promising; curious about CPU overhead.
00:13:37 Priya: overhead is higher than full cudagraph but far lower than fully dynamic; empirically we saw 10–15% CPU cost increase with sub-5% tail improvement in some workloads. we'll include exact numbers.

00:14:00 Omar: any reference docs we can read?
00:14:03 Priya: i'll share: 1) Redwood runbook for cudagraph capture + hybrid config (link: https://redwood.ai/docs/runtime/cudagraph-hybrid), 2) profiling checklist (link: https://redwood.ai/internal/prof-checklist), 3) a short notebook that runs nvtx + nsight and generates per-kernel histograms.
00:14:22 Chris: ok let's recap next steps and owners.
00:14:26 Priya: Priya to attach nvtx + cupti examples and a short annotated trace — due 2028-07-01.
00:14:32 Chris: Chris to schedule on-prem profiling with Lena for July 3.
00:14:36 Maya: Maya to upload the model artifacts + seq histogram by June 28.
00:14:40 Lena: Lena to provision ephemeral access and confirm maintenance window.

00:14:50 Omar: thanks everyone. quick question — would you recommend starting pilot on dedicated or private?
00:14:56 Priya: for this profile and control, start on Private/Dedicated where we can toggle capture_mode without affecting hosted customers. Private gives you full control over topology and driver versions. If you'd rather avoid ops work, Dedicated with reserved capacity is second choice.
00:15:12 Chris: great. we'll follow up with meeting minutes and the checklist.

00:15:20 [meeting closed — small side chatter about scheduling]

Notes: transcript contains occasional misattributions and noisy labels; some proper nouns mangled in raw capture (e.g., cupti appears as "cup ti" in nvtx labels). Shared artifacts referenced: nvtx timeline PNGs (link placeholder), nsight sys export archives, profiling checklist link.

End of transcript.
